topicTitle: 17.1 Analysis of Isotopes using Mass Spectrometry
keyPoints: Mass spectrometer ionizes sample with 70 eV electrons to produce molecular ion ($M^{+\bullet}$) with $m/z$ equal to relative molecular mass
Molecular ion peak is the highest $m/z$ value in spectrum; isotope peaks show different masses and relative abundances
Relative atomic mass calculated using: $\text{Relative atomic mass} = \frac{\sum(\text{mass} \times \text{abundance})}{100}$
Fragmentation pattern and isotopic ratios (e.g., Cl: $^{35}$Cl:$^{37}$Cl = 3:1) allow identification of elements and molecular structure
Applications include determining atomic/molecular masses, identifying isotopes, and deducing elemental composition of compounds
modelAnswer: Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique that separates ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio ($m/z$) to determine molecular and atomic masses. A sample is ionized by high-energy electrons (70 eV), producing a molecular ion ($M^{+\bullet}$) according to: $M + e^- \rightarrow M^{+\bullet} + 2e^-$. The $m/z$ value of the molecular ion peak (the highest peak in the spectrum) directly equals the relative molecular mass. The mass spectrum displays peaks corresponding to different isotopes, with peak positions revealing isotopic masses and peak heights indicating relative abundances. By analyzing the isotopic pattern and calculating the weighted average using relative abundances, the relative atomic mass is determined from the formula: $\text{Relative atomic mass} = \frac{\sum(\text{mass} \times \text{abundance})}{100}$. This technique is highly accurate and can identify elements like chlorine and bromine through their characteristic M+2 peaks, arising from their naturally occurring isotopes in approximately 3:1 ratios.

topicTitle: 17.1 Analysis of Isotopes using Mass Spectrometry
keyPoints: Mass spectrometry separates ions based on mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) to determine molecular mass
Molecules are ionized by high-energy electrons (70 eV) to form molecular ions (M⁺•) with m/z equal to relative molecular mass
Molecular ions are accelerated and separated in a magnetic field; lighter ions deflected more than heavier ions
Molecular ion peak appears at highest m/z value; fragmentation produces lower m/z peaks forming characteristic fingerprint pattern
Detector records ion abundance at each m/z value to produce mass spectrum for molecular identification
modelAnswer: Mass spectrometry is an analytical technique that separates ions based on their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) to determine molecular mass and identify molecular structure. The basic principle involves ionizing chemical compounds to generate charged molecules or fragments, then separating these ions by their m/z values using electric and/or magnetic fields. A mass spectrometer consists of an ion source, accelerating region, mass analyzer, and detector. In operation, molecules are bombarded by high-energy electrons (70 eV) in the ion source, causing loss of an electron to form molecular ions (M⁺•). These ions are accelerated through an electric field, then separated in the mass analyzer based on their m/z ratios. Lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions by the magnetic field. The detector records the abundance of ions at each m/z value, producing a mass spectrum. The molecular ion peak appears at the highest m/z value and indicates the relative molecular mass. Fragmentation of unstable molecular ions produces additional peaks at lower m/z values, creating a characteristic fragmentation pattern that serves as a fingerprint for molecular identification.

keyPoints: Correctly identifies the three isotopes and their mass numbers (24, 25, 26)
Applies weighted average formula: (mass₁ × abundance₁) + (mass₂ × abundance₂) + (mass₃ × abundance₃)
Converts percentage abundances to decimal form (78.70% = 0.7870, etc.)
Performs accurate arithmetic calculations for each term and final sum
Expresses final answer as relative atomic mass in amu (24.32 amu)
modelAnswer: The relative atomic mass of Mg is calculated using the weighted average method: Relative atomic mass = (24 × 0.7870) + (25 × 0.1013) + (26 × 0.1117) = 18.888 + 2.5325 + 2.9042 = 24.32 amu. This value represents the average mass of naturally occurring magnesium atoms accounting for the abundance of each isotope.
